comment: Per-unit question inventory for the catalog. ONE ENTRY = ONE QUESTION AT ONE LENGTH (founder decision 2026-08-20): the 8-mark Section-C forms are their own LAQ entries, each SAQ entry opens its 4-mark answer, and no card ever shows two lengths. Source for SAQ/VSAQ: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024) pp.8-12 — question text and star rank only, never its prose. The book has no LAQ section for Unit 4; the two LAQ entries are the TSBIE Basic Learning Material Section-C forms of the same derivations, numbered here for the catalog. An entry without question_id renders as a coming-soon card. build_answer_book.ts hard-fails if an authored question is missing from this file or if a question_id/cut here resolves to nothing. MATHEMATICS opens 2026-08-21 (Maths-1A). Source for its entries: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam) — question text, star rank and the PRINTED per-step mark split only, never its prose (the book's chat boxes are personified and part Telugu; Rule 41/30i). Maths-1A is a 75-mark paper: Section A Q1-Q10 VSAQ x2 (all compulsory), Section B Q11-Q17 SAQ x4 (any 5), Section C Q18-Q24 LAQ x7 (any 5). Unit numbers here are Maths-1A SYLLABUS units (1 Functions, 2 Mathematical Induction, 3 Matrices, 4 Addition of Vectors, 5 Product of Vectors, 6 Trigonometric Ratios upto Transformations, 7 Trigonometric Equations, 8 Inverse Trigonometric Functions, 9 Hyperbolic Functions, 10 Properties of Triangles) — they will COLLIDE with physics unit numbers once physics opens its Units 1-3, because this manifest has no subject dimension yet. Stars on maths LAQ entries are the CHAPTER's rank (the book stars chapters here, not individual LAQs). Unit 1 is COMPLETE: 4 LAQ (book pp.14-15) + 20 VSAQ (book pp.79-81). Functions has no SAQ chapter in this book, and none on the paper — Section B is Q11-Q17, none of which is Functions, so 24 entries IS the whole unit. VSAQ stars are the CHAPTER's rank, and the book prints no internal mark split on its VSAQ pages, so every VSAQ's 1+1 is ours, not the source's. Each unit carries a `subject`; absent means physics (physics units predate the field, the same way an appearance with no board means TS). The catalog's subject chip row appears only from the second subject on, so a physics-only build is unchanged. Unit 2 (Mathematical Induction) is COMPLETE at 8 of 8, book pp.16-21 — LAQ ONLY: the book has no induction SAQ or VSAQ chapter, and the paper has no induction question outside Section C (it is always Q19). Entry laq8 is the book's PRACTICE question, posed with no worked solution, so its answer AND its split are ours — flagged in that file's verification note. Unit 3 (Matrices) OPENS 2026-08-21 and is the largest unit on the paper: the book's chapter header reads '7+7 = 14 Marks' because Matrices holds TWO Section-C slots (Q20 and Q21), and with Q3, Q4 (VSAQ) and Q11 (SAQ) it carries 22 of the paper's 75 marks. Its full book inventory is LAQ answers 12-20 (book pp.22-34) · SAQ answers 40-45 (pp.51-55) · VSAQ answers 99-112 (pp.82-86). Its LAQ CHAPTER IS COMPLETE at 17 of 17 (book answers 12-20, pp.22-34), in four families: six determinant proofs (12-17) · four Cramer's rule (18.1-18.4) · three matrix inversion (19.1-19.3) · four Gauss-Jordan (20.1-20.4). Its SAQ CHAPTER IS ALSO COMPLETE at 9 of 9 (book answers 40-45, pp.51-55): one proof (answer 40 — the A-1 = AdjA/detA theorem, the most-asked matrices SAQ in the book at four printed appearances, and the only SAQ in the chapter carrying a PRINTED split, 1+1+1+1) · four find-the-inverse questions (41.1, 41.2, 42.1, 42.2) sharing one skeleton · two matrix-polynomial questions (43.1, 43.2) · the (aI+bE)³ identity (44) · the trigonometric product that vanishes (45). The 1+2+1 split on the four inverse SAQs is effectively SOURCED: the book asserts on p.30 that finding A-1 is worth 4 marks, and these SAQs ask for exactly that and are worth exactly 4 — so the whole question IS the book's own 4-mark chunk, divided the same way the matrix-inversion LAQs divide it. The VSAQ chapter (answers 99-112, pp.82-86) is NOT yet authored. Within each solving-a-system family the step ids, labels and mark split are deliberately IDENTICAL — the questions are one method over different numbers, the same choice Unit 2 made for induction — with ONE exception: Gauss-Jordan answers 20.3 and 20.4 do not share that skeleton, because their systems have an infinite solution set and no solution respectively, so their closing steps are a different argument rather than different numbers. Those two are the only questions in the chapter whose answer is not a single triple, and they are a matched pair: both end in a row of zero coefficients, and the ONLY thing separating them is whether the constant after the rule is zero too. Mark splits: four determinant answers carry a split PRINTED in the book's margin (12, 13, 16, 17); the matrix-inversion family carries the book's 4+3 stated in WORDS in a margin note on p.30; every other split in the unit is ours, inferred from those two, and flagged as such in each file. This is the first unit to use typeset lines (render: 'katex') heavily — 126 across the book — because a determinant and an augmented matrix have no honest one-line Unicode form.

questions.text: State the parallelogram law of vectors. Derive an expression for the magnitude and direction of the resultant vector.
Show that the trajectory of a projectile is a parabola. Derive expressions for its time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range.
State the parallelogram law of vectors. Derive an expression for the magnitude and direction of the resultant vector.
Show that the maximum height and range of a projectile are u²sin²θ/2g and u²sin2θ/g respectively.
Define unit vector, null vector and position vector.
Show that the trajectory of an object thrown at an angle with the horizontal is a parabola.
Show that for a projectile launched at an angle of 45° the maximum height of the projectile is one quarter of the range.
If |a + b| = |a − b|, prove that the angle between a and b is 90°.

Two balls are projected from the same point in directions 30° and 60° with respect to the horizontal. What is the ratio of their initial velocities if they (a) attain the same height (b) have the same range?
Explain the terms average velocity and instantaneous velocity. When are they equal?
O is a point on the ground chosen as origin. A body first suffers a displacement of 10√2 m north-east, next 10 m north and finally 10√2 m north-west. How far is it from the origin?
The vertical component of a vector is equal to its horizontal component. What is the angle made by the vector with the x-axis?
A vector V makes an angle with the horizontal. The vector is rotated through an angle α. Does this rotation change the vector V?
Two forces of magnitudes 3 units and 5 units act at 60° with each other. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
A = i + j. What is the angle between the vector and the x-axis?
If P = 2i + 4j + 14k and Q = 4i + 4j + 10k, find the magnitude of P + Q.
Can a vector of magnitude zero have non-zero components?
What is the acceleration of a projectile at the top of its trajectory?
When two right-angled vectors of magnitude 7 units and 24 units combine, what is the magnitude of their resultant?

A man walks on a straight road from his home to a market 2.5 km away with a speed of 5 km/h. Finding the market closed, he instantly turns and walks back home with a speed of 7.5 km/h. What is (a) the magnitude of the average velocity and (b) the average speed of the man over the interval 0 to 50 min?
If f: A→B, g: B→C are two bijective functions then prove that gof: A→C is also a bijective function.
If f: A→B, g: B→C are two bijective functions then prove that (gof)⁻¹ = f⁻¹og⁻¹.
If f: A→B is a function and I_A, I_B are identity functions on A, B respectively then prove that foI_A = f = I_Bof.
If f: A→B is a bijective function then prove that (i) fof⁻¹ = I_B (ii) f⁻¹of = I_A.
If f: R→R, g: R→R are defined by f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 1, then find (fog)(2).
If f(x) = 2x − 1, g(x) = (x + 1)/2 for all x ∈ R, find (i) (gof)(x) (ii) (fog)(x).
If A = {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2} and f: A→B is a surjection defined by f(x) = x² + x + 1 then find B.
If A = {0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2} and f: A→B is a surjection defined by f(x) = cos x then find B.
If f: Q→Q is defined by f(x) = 5x + 4, find f⁻¹.
Find the inverse of the real function f(x) = ax + b, a ≠ 0.
Find the inverse function of f(x) = 5ˣ.
Find the inverse function of f(x) = log₂x.
Find the domain of the real function √(9 − x²).
Find the domain of the real function √(16 − x²).
Find the domain of the real function √(x² − 25).
Find the domain of the real function √(x² − 3x + 2).
Find the domain of the real function log(x² − 4x + 3).
Find the domain of the real function 1/√(x² − a²).
Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(4x − x²).
Find the domain of the real function 1/√(1 − x²).
Find the domain of the real function 1/((x² − 1)(x + 3)).
Find the domain of the real function (2x² − 5x + 7)/((x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3)).
Using the principle of finite Mathematical Induction prove that 1·2·3 + 2·3·4 + 3·4·5 + … upto n terms = n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)/4, ∀ n ∈ N.
Using the principle of finite Mathematical Induction prove that 1² + (1² + 2²) + (1² + 2² + 3²) + … n terms = n(n+1)²(n+2)/12, ∀ n ∈ N.
By Mathematical Induction, show that 49ⁿ + 16n − 1 is divisible by 64 for all positive integers n.
Using the principle of Mathematical Induction, prove that 3·5⁽²ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + 2⁽³ⁿ⁺¹⁾ is divisible by 17, ∀ n ∈ N.
Using P.M.I, show that 2·4⁽²ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + 3⁽³ⁿ⁺¹⁾ is divisible by 11, ∀ n ∈ N.
Show that the determinant with rows (a, b, c), (a², b², c²) and (a³, b³, c³) is equal to abc(a−b)(b−c)(c−a).
Show that the determinant with rows (1, a², a³), (1, b², b³) and (1, c², c³) is equal to (a−b)(b−c)(c−a)(ab+bc+ca).
Show that the determinant with rows (a+b+2c, a, b), (c, b+c+2a, b) and (c, a, c+a+2b) is equal to 2(a+b+c)³.
Show that the determinant with rows (a−b−c, 2a, 2a), (2b, b−c−a, 2b) and (2c, 2c, c−a−b) is equal to (a+b+c)³.

Show that the square of the determinant with rows (a, b, c), (b, c, a) and (c, a, b) equals the determinant with rows (2bc−a², c², b²), (c², 2ac−b², a²) and (b², a², 2ab−c²), and that both equal (a³+b³+c³−3abc)².
Show that the determinant with rows (b+c, c+a, a+b), (c+a, a+b, b+c) and (a+b, b+c, c+a) is equal to twice the determinant with rows (a, b, c), (b, c, a) and (c, a, b).
By using Cramer's rule, solve 2x − y + 3z = 9, x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2.
By using Cramer's rule, solve 3x + 4y + 5z = 18, 2x − y + 8z = 13, 5x − 2y + 7z = 20.

By using Cramer's rule, solve x − y + 3z = 5, 4x + 2y − z = 0, x + 3y + z = 5.

By using the matrix inversion method, solve 3x + 4y + 5z = 18, 2x − y + 8z = 13, 5x − 2y + 7z = 20.

By the Gauss-Jordan method, solve 2x + 4y − z = 0, x + 2y + 2z = 5, 3x + 6y − 7z = 2.
If A is a non-singular matrix, then prove that A⁻¹ = (Adj A)/(det A).
Find the adjoint and the inverse of the matrix A with rows (1, 3, 3), (1, 4, 3) and (1, 3, 4).
Find the adjoint and the inverse of the matrix A with rows (1, 0, 2), (2, 1, 0) and (3, 2, 1).

If θ − φ = π/2, then show that the product of the matrix with rows (cos²θ, cosθ sinθ) and (cosθ sinθ, sin²θ) with the matrix with rows (cos²φ, cosφ sinφ) and (cosφ sinφ, sin²φ) is the zero matrix O.
